newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China brings volatility to Hong Kong stock market.
newsitem.headline: China brings volatility to Hong Kong stock market.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks have taken a roller-coaster ride this year, driven by handover optimism and China's red chip stocks, although volatility could become more frequent with the mainland's resumption of sovereignty.
"A greater Chinese involvement in the Hong Kong market is definitely to be expected in the future," Jake van der Kamp, investment strategist at HG Asia, said on Tuesday.
"It is an emerging market, it is an emerging economy and capital flows in emerging economies tend to be more volatile," he said.
Chinese companies are now playing an increasing role on the Hong Kong stock market through the listing of red chip shares -- stocks of Hong Kong-based companies with mainland parents.

"Where more Chinese companies are listing and disclosure is not as clear cut, that could create an atmosphere of greater volatility and uncertainty," said Peter Churchouse, managing director at Morgan Stanley Asia.

Prospects of asset injections by Chinese parents have sparked a speculative frenzy in these high growth shares, but with price earnings multiples of more than 30 times, it is sentiment, not fundamentals, which is driving their prices.

"They are valued more on their potential than their existing performance," said Andrew Fernow, director of reseach at Vickers Ballas. "There will always be volatility due to the new, more conceptual types of stocks that make up the group."
Along with the speculative money flowing into the red chip shares, hot money from China has found its way to Hong Kong ahead of China's takeover on July 1, analysts said.

"Increasingly it seems that the market is going to become more accessible to the PRC (People's Republic of China) and in theory that should increase liquidity in the Hong Kong market," Churchouse said.

While China cooled the flow of hot money into Hong Kong earlier this month with a ban on state banks trading in stocks, and made a move last week to tighten control on overseas listings and asset injections, red chips are set to remain a strong investment theme.

Stock Exchange of Hong Kong chairman Edgar Cheng welcomed the shift in market characteristics, although he used Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's famous "irrational exuberance" phrase to describe the fever sweeping Hong Kong.

"It reflects local and international expectations about the prospects for mainland-backed companies listed in Hong Kong. It may also reflect indirectly a new interest on the part of mainland investors in our market," he told a Far Eastern Economic Review seminar this week.
"Participation of a new pool of investors should add diversity and liquidity to the market, even if it brings greater volatility to some sectors in the short term," he said.
As Hong Kong share prices scale higher in the months ahead analysts said volatility was also bound to increase.
The Hang Seng blue chip index has traded between a low of 11,951.94 points and an all-time high of 15,322.33 this year.
On Tuesday it fell 130.27 points to close at 14,890.96 after swinging between a high of 15,028.73 and a low of 14,797.11.

"I see in the coming 12 months the Hong Kong market will probably go into this final bull phase," said Percy Au-young, director of research at DBS Securities "The rise will be very steep and the volatility will be very high."
